Well of Living Waters
WEL uv LIV-ing WAW-terz
n. phr. (the bridegroom's figure for the bride, a spring of running water)
Hebrew be'er mayim chayyim — be'er, a dug well or pit; mayim chayyim, living waters, the Hebrew term for water that runs and is not stagnant, required for certain purifications in the law.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

The bridegroom praises his bride in a run of three figures: “A fountain of gardens, a well of living waters, and streams from Lebanon.” The phrase before it — a garden inclosed, a spring shut up, a fountain sealed — has just named her exclusiveness; now the same water is named for its quality. Living water in Hebrew usage is not a metaphor for vitality in general but a technical description: water that moves, fed from a source, as distinguished from the still water of a cistern. The law required running water for the cleansing of the leper and for the water of separation, so the phrase carries the sense of water fit for purifying. Three things follow. The bride is a source and not a reservoir; her waters are her husband's and sealed to him; and what comes from her is fresh and cleansing rather than kept and stagnant. Scripture takes up the same figure elsewhere and raises it. The LORD indicts His people for forsaking Him, the fountain of living waters, to hew out broken cisterns; Christ offers the woman at the well water springing up into everlasting life; and He promises that out of the believer's belly shall flow rivers of living water, which John says was spoken of the Spirit.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): Well, a spring; a fountain; a pit dug to obtain water. Living, in Scripture, running, as living water, in distinction from stagnant. A well of living waters, Song of Solomon 4:15, the bridegroom's figure for his bride.

Well, a spring or fountain; a pit or hole dug in the earth to obtain water.

Living, having life; of water, running or springing, not stagnant.

Hebrew be'er, a well dug or sunk to reach water beneath.

Hebrew mayim chayyim, living waters, that is, running and not still.

Required for the cleansing of the leper, Leviticus 14:5.

Key Scripture

Son 4:15 — "A fountain of gardens, a well of living waters, and streams from Lebanon."

Son 4:12 — "A garden inclosed is my sister, my spouse; a spring shut up, a fountain sealed."

Joh 4:14 — "But whosoever drinketh of the water that I shall give him shall never thirst; but the water that I shall give him shall be in him a well of water springing up into everlasting life."

Joh 7:38 — "He that believeth on me, as the scripture hath said, out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water."

Modern Corruption

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition, though the figure is often spiritualized so quickly that the Song's own subject — a wife praised by her husband — disappears.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. No rival doctrine attaches to the phrase. The besetting fault is a devotional one, and it runs in two directions. Some expositors move so fast to the allegory that the Song's plain subject is never allowed to stand — a bridegroom praising his own wife in terms of running water, sealed to him and cleansing — and a book God gave to sanctify marriage ends up never applied to a marriage. Others, reacting, refuse the typology altogether and leave the Song in the bedroom, as though Scripture's long use of marriage for Christ and His church began with Paul.

The principle to recover is the order the Reformed expositors kept. The literal sense comes first and is honoured: this is a husband's praise of his wife, and Christian husbands are to speak so. The typical sense is then real and not invented, because Scripture itself makes marriage the figure of Christ and the church, and the same living-water language is taken up by Christ at the well and in the temple courts, and by the LORD in Jeremiah against those who forsake the fountain of living waters for broken cisterns. Read in that order the phrase enriches both a marriage and a soul; read in either half alone it is impoverished.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew be'er, a dug well; mayim chayyim, living — that is, running — water, the law's requirement for cleansing the leper and for the water of separation.

Hebrew be'er, a well sunk or dug to reach the water beneath.

Hebrew mayim chayyim, living waters: running, fed from a source, not stagnant.

Hebrew gan na'ul, a garden inclosed, the preceding figure, Song 4:12.

Running water was required for cleansing the leper, Leviticus 14:5.

Taken up of the Spirit by Christ in the temple, John 7:38-39.
